newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan's dependence on Middle East crude rising.
newsitem.headline: Japan's dependence on Middle East crude rising.

text.p: Japan's reliance on crude oil imports from the Middle East is at its highest level in 24 years, despite a long-term policy to diversify the source of its supplies.
And analysts say Japan's already heavy dependence on the Middle East will grow over time as Asian crude exports fall.

"With Japan's oil demand set to rise while supplies of regional crudes are forecast to decline, it is inevitable that reliance on the Middle East will grow," an official with the overseas operations department of Idemitsu Kosan Co Ltd said.
"Some refiners are expected to increase their annual term contract volumes of Middle Eastern crudes," he said.
Japan is Asia's biggest consumer of crude oil and with few energy sources of its own, is almost entirely dependent on imports.
In 1996, Middle Eastern crudes accounted for 80 percent of Japan's total imports of 263.4 million kilolitres (1.657 billion barrels), the Ministry of International Trade and Industry (MITI) said.
It is the first time in 24 years that dependence on the Middle East, most noteably Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, has risen above 80 percent, MITI said.

Japan has operated a long-term policy of seeking oil supplies from outside the Middle East since the oil shocks of the 1970s and 1980s when prices skyrocketed. The 1990/1991 Gulf War added to worries of supply security.
Following the policy, Middle East imports fell as low as 67.4 percent in 1987, but they have been on the rise ever since, MITI data shows.

But today, Japanese buyers said they were more relaxed about Middle East crude, since varous peace initiatives were launched. "The Middle East has stabalised and we consider the region as a reliable supplier with immense reserves," the Idemitsu official said. The Middle East holds about 65 percent or world proven oil reserves.
"Asia as a whole is expected to need to rely more on the Middle East for supplies, and in the near future, Asian countries may need to compete for Middle Eastern crude," he said.
More Japanese buyers are looking to lock in long-term contracts after the spot market value for Middle East crudes rose sharply last year.
Abu Dhabi's Murban crude was constantly traded at a premium to the official selling price (OSP) through 1996, achieving a premium as high as 80 cents by the end of the year.
This was in sharp contrast to 1995 when Murban traded between a 30-cent discount to a 45-cent premium in relation to the OSP.
But since Japan's oil imports were liberalised in 1996, some buyers said they gave priority to flexiblity, which could only be achieved through trading on the spot market.
Also for economic reasons, relatively heavy high-sulphur Middle Eastern crudes, produced by the likes of Iran and Kuwait, are gaining popularity, traders said.
Crude imports from Kuwait rose seven percent in 1996 to 13.8 million kl from a year earlier and Iranian crude imports rose 13.5 percent to 26 million kl, MITI said.
Heavy, high-sulphur crudes are generally cheaper compared to light low-sulphur crudes.

"It can be said that heavier grades are growing popular because of the low price and also because refiners want to operate their secondary refining equipment at full to enhance economic efficiency," a trader with a refiner said.
